Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds as a vivid, real-time scene, following Vera as she unlocks the door, steps into the hallway, and walks into the kitchen. The author uses rich sensory details (the sound of the lock, the smell of mothballs and turpentine, the grey November light) to ground the reader in the present action. At the same time, the writer seamlessly weaves in brief, crucial pieces of exposition—such as the fact that Vera hasn't been there in twenty years, that the house belonged to her mother Helga, and that her mother died two weeks ago and hadn't painted in thirty years. Instead of slowing the story down with a dry info-dump, this background information is delivered precisely when needed to heighten the tension and create the final mystery of the fresh paint in the sink.
